Rib fractures—especially of ribs 2–5—are also extremely common in blunt anterior chest trauma and often co-occur (0.88). Myocardial contusion is less frequent but clinically significant; it occurs in ~10–20% of major blunt chest trauma cases and may present with chest pain, ECG changes, or troponin elevation (0.75). Pneumothorax is a frequent complication of rib/sternum fractures or direct lung parenchymal injury and may be occult on initial exam (0.72). Blunt thoracic aortic injury (BTAI), though rarer (~1–2% of major trauma), carries high mortality if missed; it classically follows rapid deceleration and may present with isolated chest/back pain—thus warrants urgent exclusion despite lower pretest probability (0.65). Sternal fracture is highly likely given its strong association with dashboard or steering wheel impact in restrained drivers; it commonly presents with localized, reproducible sternal tenderness and pain on palpation or deep inspiration. Rib fractures are also extremely common in blunt chest trauma and often co-occur; they typically cause sharp, pleuritic, or movement-exacerbated pain. Myocardial contusion must be considered due to the potential for hemodynamic instability, arrhythmias, or elevated troponins—though absence of crepitus makes overt chest wall disruption less likely, it does not exclude myocardial injury. Pulmonary contusion is frequent after high-speed deceleration and may present with dyspnea, hypoxia, or radiographic infiltrates even before symptoms escalate. Traumatic aortic injury remains a critical 'can't miss' diagnosis—especially with rapid deceleration—but is less common than bony or soft-tissue injuries; its lower confidence reflects the absence of classic red flags (e.g., pulse deficit, widened mediastinum on CXR, severe hypertension), though clinical suspicion must remain high pending imaging."}
